caption:
Can't fall asleep? Shower 90 minutes before bed. A warm shower, timed right, helps you fall asleep sooner.

WHY: warm water sends blood out to your hands and feet. Afterwards your body lets that heat go and your core temperature drops, and that drop is one of the signals your body uses to start sleep.

HOW:
1. Pick your bedtime (say 11 pm).
2. Count back about 90 minutes (9:30 pm). Anywhere from 1 to 2 hours before bed works.
3. Warm, not hot: about 40 to 42.5 °C (104 to 108.5 °F). A bath works too.
4. 10 minutes in the water is enough.

THE RESEARCH: a review of 17 studies (13 with data to combine) found that warm showers or baths 1 to 2 hours before bed shortened the time it took to fall asleep, even with as little as 10 minutes in the water. People also rated their sleep as better.

THE CATCH: the studies were small, and the timing matters. A hot shower right before bed hasn't had time to cool you down. It helps you drift off; it is not a treatment for insomnia.

Do this tonight: Bed at 11? Shower warm at 9:30. 10 minutes in the water is enough.

Send this to whoever is still scrolling at midnight because they can't drop off.

Part 2 is tomorrow (Monday) at 7 pm: the lamp. Why ordinary room light in the evening tells your body it's still daytime, and the one switch to flip after dinner.

Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#sleep #bedtimeroutine #focus #habits #sleepbetter

caption:
Your ceiling light says it's daytime. After dinner, switch to one small lamp.

Fall asleep sooner, Part 2. (Part 1, yesterday: a warm shower about 90 minutes before bed.)

WHY: melatonin is the hormone your body releases when it decides it's night. It starts to rise in the evening, a couple of hours before you usually fall asleep. Ordinary indoor light, the kind from a ceiling light, holds it back, so your body's night starts later.

HOW:
1. After dinner, turn off the big overhead light.
2. Use one small lamp, low and warm, for the rest of the evening.
3. Keep it that way until bed. (Your phone screen is light too: turn it down.)

THE RESEARCH: in a lab study, young adults spent the 8 hours before bed either in ordinary room light or in dim light. In room light, the body's "it's night" signal (melatonin) lasted about 90 minutes less, and started later in 99% of them.

THE CATCH: the study measured melatonin, not how fast people fell asleep, and it was a lab study with healthy 18 to 30 year olds over 8 hours of light. Dimming for your evening is a sensible way to use it, not something the study tested exactly.

Do this tonight: Big light off. One small lamp on.

Send this to whoever keeps every light in the house on until midnight.

Follow for one small focus trick a day.

caption:
Studying tonight? 24 minutes on, 6 off: set a timer for your breaks. Planned breaks keep you fresher than breaking whenever you feel like it.

WHY: when you wait until you feel tired, you tend to push past the point where focus is already slipping, and then take a long break to recover. A timer decides for you, so you stop before you're drained.

HOW:
1. Pick one task (one chapter, one problem set).
2. Set a timer for 24 minutes. Work until it rings.
3. When it rings, really stop: 6 minutes. Stand up, stretch, get water. No phone.
4. Reset the timer for the next round.

THE RESEARCH: 87 university students did a self-study session. Some took breaks whenever they wanted; others had timed breaks (24 minutes on, 6 off, or 12 on, 3 off). The students on timed breaks reported less fatigue, better concentration and more motivation, and, in the authors' words, reached 'similar task completion in shorter time'. The ones who chose their own breaks took longer breaks.

THE CATCH: one study, one session, with feelings measured by self-report. Timed breaks didn't make students finish more tasks; they finished the same work feeling fresher.

Do this tonight: Timer: 24 minutes on, 6 off. That's the timing from the study (not a typo for 25). Then the next round.

Send this to whoever is about to pull a 'no breaks' study night.

Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#studytips #focus #pomodoro #studywithme #deepwork

Source (checked Nov 1 2026 on the Maastricht University research portal record and the PubMed record, PMID 36859717):
Biwer, F., Wiradhany, W., oude Egbrink, M. G. A. & de Bruin, A. B. H. (2023). Understanding effort regulation: Comparing 'Pomodoro' breaks and self-regulated breaks. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 93(S2), 353–367. 87 bachelor's and master's students; self-regulated breaks (n=35) vs systematic breaks: 6 min after every 24 min (n=25) or 3 min after every 12 min (n=27). Self-regulated breaks went with higher fatigue and distractedness and lower concentration and motivation; task completion and mental effort did not differ; the Conclusions state systematic breaks gave 'similar task completion in shorter time' (re-checked Nov 1 on the ERIC record EJ1386535); self-regulators took longer breaks.
Limits: one study session; self-reported fatigue, concentration and motivation; the abstract gives directions, not sizes, so the Reel shows no numbers for them.

caption:
Boring call? Grab a pen. Today's word: Doodle.

One Word No. 6. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: on a dull call your mind drifts off. Simple doodling gives it just enough to do to stay in the room, without pulling your attention away from what's being said.

THE RESEARCH: 40 people listened to a dull 2.5-minute phone message and wrote down the names of people coming to a party. Half also filled in printed squares and circles while they listened. The doodlers caught more names, and in a surprise memory test they remembered 29% more: 7.5 details on average against 5.8.

HOW:
1. Before a long call, meeting or lecture, put a pen and a scrap of paper in front of you.
2. While you listen, fill in simple shapes: boxes, circles, lines.
3. Keep it simple. A detailed drawing becomes its own task.

THE CATCH: it's one small study with a boring message, and the doodling was filling in simple shapes. Drawing something you have to think about, or doodling on your phone, isn't the same thing.

Do this: Long call or lecture? Keep a pen and paper. Fill in simple shapes while you listen.

Send this to whoever has a 90-minute meeting tomorrow.

One Word No. 7 is Friday at 5 pm.

Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#focus #memory #doodle #productivity #oneword

Source (checked Nov 1 2026 on the author's accepted manuscript, University of Plymouth repository):
Andrade, J. (2010). What does doodling do? Applied Cognitive Psychology, 24(1), 100–106. doi:10.1002/acp.1561. 40 participants (20 doodling, 20 control), aged 18–55, monitored a monotonous mock telephone message (about 2.5 minutes) for the names of people coming to a party; the doodling group shaded printed squares and circles while listening. Abstract: 'The doodling group performed better on the monitoring task and recalled 29% more information on a surprise memory test.' Mean recall 7.5 vs 5.8 items (names 5.3 vs 4.3; places 2.6 vs 2.1).
Limits: one small study; simple shading, not free drawing; the mechanism (less daydreaming or more arousal) is the author's suggestion for future work.
